title: Single-use devices, symbols & prion risk
blurb: What the crossed-out 2 means, why single-use items are never reprocessed, and how prions shape the rules for endodontic files.
question: During a stock check, a new colleague suggests putting this morning's used saliva ejectors and the endodontic files from a root canal treatment through the sterilizer 'to save money'. What do you tell them, and why?

teach.body: HTM 01-05 is clear: a single-use device is used during one treatment episode and then disposed of. It is not intended to be reprocessed and used again, not even on the same patient at a later appointment. Single-use items are identified by a symbol: the number 2 inside a circle with a line through it, meaning 'do not reuse'. It appears on the packaging, but might not be on the item itself, so check the packaging before you open it.

root.label: Check the packaging first
root.sub: The symbol may not be on the item

children.label: Single use or single patient use, whatever the label says

teach.caption: If in doubt about an item's status, HTM 01-05 says ask the manufacturer.

teach.h: Why single-use items are never reprocessed
teach.body: The manufacturer has not designed or tested the item to survive cleaning and sterilisation. Narrow tubes may be impossible to clean inside, plastics may warp or crack in the heat, and fine metal may weaken. So its safety and performance can't be guaranteed after reprocessing. There's a legal side too: under the Medical Devices Regulations, anyone who reprocesses a device marked for single use takes on the manufacturer's responsibility for its safety and effectiveness.

teach.h: Single use, single patient use, reusable
teach.caption: HTM 01-05 says reusable endodontic files and reamers must be treated as single use or single patient use, whatever the manufacturer says, with systems to link each one to the right patient.

teach.h: Hard-to-clean items: make them single use

Status
Why
teach.caption: HTM 01-05 names these as examples. Where any instrument can't be cleaned reliably, consider a single-use version.

teach.h: Prions: the infection that sterilisation can't fully kill
teach.body: Prions are abnormal infectious proteins that cause diseases such as variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD). A carrier may have no symptoms at all, so you can't tell who is affected. HTM 01-05 says no recognised process fully deactivates prion protein. Steam sterilisation reduces their infectivity usefully, but the real defence is washing protein off before sterilising. Evidence suggests the risk is most pronounced in endodontic work, which is why endodontic files became single use or single patient use.

steps.label: Prion protein on an instrument
steps.sub: Possible after contact with dental tissue

steps.label: Single use where cleaning is hard

teach.caption: Because carriers can't be identified, these measures are applied to every patient.

teach.h: Before you open a single-use item
teach.body: Check three things. The symbol: is it single use? The packaging: is it intact and dry? The expiry (use-by) date: sterility and the material's performance are only assured up to that date, so an out-of-date item isn't used. Store sterile single-use stock clean and dry, and keep it separate from used instruments waiting to be decontaminated. After use, single-use items go into the correct waste stream, never back into the decontamination room.

teach.text: 'Single use' and 'single patient use' are not the same. A single-use device is thrown away after one treatment episode: you can't clean it and use it on the same patient next week. Only an item designated single patient use may be reprocessed for that one patient.

items: Crossed-out 2 = single use: one treatment episode, then dispose. Never reprocess.
Reprocessing makes you responsible for the device's safety under the Medical Devices Regulations.
Endodontic files and reamers: single use or single patient use, whatever the label says.
Prions aren't fully deactivated by any process; thorough cleaning plus steam reduces the risk.
Check symbol, packaging and expiry date before opening.

summary: You can now recognise the single-use symbol, explain why single-use devices are never reprocessed (including the legal reason), tell single use from single patient use, explain why prions make thorough cleaning and single-use endodontic files so important, and check single-use items before opening them.

A.q: Which symbol on packaging shows that an item is single use?
options: A number 2 in a circle, crossed through
An hourglass with a date beside it
A wheelie bin with a cross through it
A black flame inside a red-bordered diamond
A.why: The single-use ('do not reuse') symbol is a 2 in a circle with a line through it.

whyNot.1: An hourglass shows the use-by (expiry) date.
whyNot.2: A crossed-out wheelie bin relates to electrical waste disposal.
whyNot.3: A flame in a red diamond is the COSHH flammable pictogram.

A.q: Why must a device marked single use never be reprocessed?
options: It would take too long to clean
Its safety and performance can't be guaranteed
It would fill the sterilizer too quickly
It is made of glass that shatters when heated
A.why: Single-use devices aren't designed or validated to survive reprocessing, so their safety and effectiveness after it can't be guaranteed.

whyNot.0: Time isn't the reason; safety and performance are.
whyNot.3: Single-use items are made of many materials, mostly plastics and metals, not glass.

A.q: Under HTM 01-05, how should endodontic files designated as reusable by the manufacturer be treated?
options: Reused on any patient after sterilising
Sterilised twice before reuse
Soaked in disinfectant overnight
As single use or single patient use
A.why: To reduce the risk of prion transmission, HTM 01-05 says reusable endodontic files and reamers are treated as single use or single patient use, whatever the manufacturer's designation.

whyNot.0: Reuse between patients is exactly what the guidance prevents.
whyNot.1: Extra sterilisation doesn't reliably deactivate prions.
whyNot.2: Chemical soaking is not an accepted alternative.

B.q: A single-use matrix band was used on a patient this morning. They return next week for the same tooth. Can the band be cleaned and reused for them?
options: Yes, if it is sterilised in a pouch
Yes, because it is the same patient
No, single use means one episode only
No, unless the dentist approves it first
B.why: HTM 01-05 says a single-use device is used in one treatment episode and disposed of, not reused even on the same patient later.

whyNot.0: Sterilising doesn't change a single-use device's status.
whyNot.1: Same patient makes no difference for single-use items.
whyNot.3: The dentist can't override the device's single-use designation.

B.q: What is the legal consequence of reprocessing a device CE-marked for single use?
options: The practice must notify the GDC
You take on the maker's responsibilities
The device may then be stored for one year
The patient must sign a consent form
B.why: Under the Medical Devices Regulations, whoever reprocesses a single-use device bears the responsibilities normally carried by the manufacturer for its safety and effectiveness.

whyNot.0: There is no GDC notification route that makes this acceptable.
whyNot.2: Reprocessing doesn't create any storage allowance.
whyNot.3: Patient consent doesn't make reprocessing a single-use device acceptable.

B.q: Why is prion contamination a particular concern for instrument decontamination?
options: Prions are killed by cold water
Prions only affect dental staff
No process fully deactivates prion protein
Prions are easily seen under an illuminated magnifier
B.why: HTM 01-05 notes there is no recognised process that can fully deactivate prion protein, so thorough cleaning plus steam sterilisation is used to reduce the risk.

whyNot.1: The concern is transmission between patients via instruments.
whyNot.3: Prions are proteins far too small to see; inspection checks for visible soil.

C.q: Why should you check the expiry date on a sterile single-use item before opening it?
options: Sterility is only assured up to that date
It shows when the item was manufactured
It tells you how many times it can be used
It is needed for the waste consignment note
C.why: The manufacturer only assures sterility and material performance up to the expiry date.

whyNot.1: The expiry date is a use-by date, not the date of manufacture.
whyNot.2: Single-use items can only be used once, whatever the date.
whyNot.3: Expiry dates aren't recorded on waste consignment notes.

C.q: Which of these items does HTM 01-05 suggest replacing with single-use versions because they are difficult to clean?
options: Dental mirrors
Extraction forceps
Aspirator tips
Amalgam pluggers
C.why: HTM 01-05 lists matrix bands, saliva ejectors, aspirator tips and three-in-one tips as examples of hard-to-clean items to consider making single use.

whyNot.0: Mirrors are routinely reprocessed in a validated cycle.
whyNot.1: Forceps are reusable instruments with open hinges for cleaning.
whyNot.3: Pluggers are solid hand instruments that can be cleaned and sterilised.

C.q: Where should you look to be sure of finding the single-use symbol?
options: Engraved on the handle
On the item's packaging
On the sterilizer print-out
Inside the instrument lumen
C.why: HTM 01-05 says the symbol appears on the packaging but might not be on individual items, so check the packaging before use.

whyNot.0: Many single-use items carry no marking on the item itself.
whyNot.2: Sterilizer print-outs record cycles, not device status.

reteach.title: Think of a paper cup and a china mug
reteach.question: You wouldn't put a paper coffee cup through the dishwasher and hand it to the next customer. Why not, and how does that apply to dental devices?

blocks.body: A china mug is made to be washed hundreds of times. A paper cup is made to be used once: put it through a hot wash and it goes soggy, leaks and falls apart. Single-use dental devices are the paper cups. They aren't built to survive cleaning and steam, so after reprocessing nobody can promise they're clean inside, still strong or still working. The crossed-out 2 on the packet is the manufacturer saying 'this is a paper cup'.

blocks.text: Sterilising a single-use item doesn't turn it into a reusable one. Its status comes from the manufacturer's design, not from what you do to it afterwards.

explain.body: A 2 inside a circle with a line through it means single use: use once, during one treatment episode, then dispose of it. It's on the packaging and may not be on the item.

test.q: What does the crossed-out 2 symbol on a packet mean?
options: Use within two days
Single use only
Two items inside
Sterilise twice
test.why: The crossed-out 2 is the 'do not reuse' symbol for single-use devices.

whyNot.3: Single-use items are never reprocessed at all.

explain.body: Not designed or validated for reprocessing: may be impossible to clean, may warp or weaken. Safety and performance can't be guaranteed, and the reprocessor takes on the manufacturer's legal responsibilities.

test.q: Which regulations place the manufacturer's responsibilities on anyone who reprocesses a single-use device?
options: The Medical Devices Regulations
The Ionising Radiations Regulations
The Hazardous Waste Regulations
The Data Protection Act
test.why: HTM 01-05 explains that reprocessing a single-use device has implications under the Medical Devices Regulations.

whyNot.2: These govern hazardous waste, not device reuse.

explain.body: Infectious proteins (for example vCJD). Carriers can be symptom-free. No process fully deactivates them, so thorough cleaning and validated steam are both essential, and endodontic files are single use or single patient use.

test.q: Which dental instruments are most closely linked with the prion risk guidance in HTM 01-05?
options: Endodontic files and reamers
Dental mirrors
Impression trays
Bib clips
test.why: Evidence suggests the prion risk is most pronounced in endodontic work, so files and reamers are treated as single use or single patient use.

whyNot.2: Impression trays aren't the focus of the prion guidance.
whyNot.3: Bib clips don't contact the dental tissues linked to prion risk.

explain.body: Symbol (single use?), packaging (intact and dry?), expiry date (sterility is assured only until then). Out of date or damaged: don't use it.

test.q: A sterile single-use item's packet is intact but it expired last month. What should you do?
options: Use it, as the packet is sealed
Sterilise it, then use it
Do not use it
Use it on a low-risk patient
test.why: Sterility and performance are only assured up to the expiry date, so an expired single-use item is not used.

whyNot.0: An intact packet doesn't extend the expiry date.
